objectives: Trace the founding of audiology from Bell Labs psychoacoustics to post-WWII clinical practice.
Read a pure-tone audiogram: dB HL versus frequency from 250 Hz to 8 kHz.
Name the key figures (Fletcher, Munson, von Bekesy, Carhart) and what each contributed.

slides.title: Where audiology came from
slides.body:
**Audiology** is the science and clinical profession concerned with hearing, balance, and their disorders. It sits at the intersection of physics (acoustics), physiology (the auditory system), and clinical medicine. Unlike many medical specialties, audiology has an unusually precise origin: it was forged from **psychoacoustics** research at the **Bell Telephone Laboratories** in the 1920s and 1930s and from the rehabilitation needs of soldiers returning from **World War II**.

The telephone created a commercial reason to quantify hearing. To engineer a phone line, **Bell Labs** needed to know how loud a signal must be for an average listener to hear it, and how that threshold changed with **frequency**. **Harvey Fletcher (1884-1981)**, often called the *father of stereophonic sound*, led much of this work and wrote the landmark book *Speech and Hearing* (1929). With his colleague **Wilden A. Munson**, Fletcher published the **equal-loudness contours** in 1933, mapping how the perceived loudness of pure tones depends on both their physical level and their frequency.

Meanwhile, the basic biophysics of the inner ear was being unraveled by the Hungarian-born physicist **Georg von Bekesy (1899-1972)**, who showed experimentally that a sound entering the cochlea sets up a **traveling wave** along the **basilar membrane**, with the position of peak vibration depending on frequency. For this work von Bekesy received the **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1961** — still the only Nobel awarded primarily for hearing research.

The clinical profession itself crystallized after WWII. **Raymond Carhart (1912-1975)** at **Northwestern University**, working with veterans deafened by gunfire and blast, is widely regarded as the **father of clinical audiology**. He coined much of the early terminology, formalized aural rehabilitation, and trained the first generation of clinical audiologists. The very word *audiology* dates to roughly **1946**. In one generation hearing science moved from the laboratory bench at **Bell Labs** to a recognized clinical discipline practiced in hospitals and rehabilitation centers, and the central diagnostic tool of that discipline became the **audiogram**.

slides.title: Reading the audiogram
slides.body:
The **audiogram** is the single most important graph in clinical audiology. It is a chart of a person's **hearing threshold** — the quietest sound they can just detect — as a function of **frequency**. Understanding its axes is essential.

The **horizontal axis** is frequency in **hertz (Hz)**, plotted on a logarithmic scale, conventionally from **250 Hz** on the left to **8000 Hz (8 kHz)** on the right, with octave steps at 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 4000, and 8000 Hz (and often half-octave points at 750, 1500, 3000, and 6000 Hz). These frequencies were chosen because they span the range most important for understanding **speech**. Low frequencies carry vowels and the fundamental of the voice; high frequencies carry consonants such as /s/, /f/, and /th/ that distinguish words.

The **vertical axis** is the threshold in **decibels Hearing Level (dB HL)**, and crucially it is plotted *upside down*: **0 dB HL is at the top** and louder, poorer thresholds run **downward**. The reason is the calibration. **dB HL** is referenced to the average threshold of young, healthy, normally hearing adults — a standard codified in **ANSI S3.6** and **ISO 389**. By definition, an audiometrically normal young listener scores about **0 dB HL** at every frequency. So the closer the trace is to the top of the chart, the better the hearing.

Thresholds are obtained by **pure-tone audiometry**: the audiologist presents a single sine-wave tone through calibrated headphones (air conduction) or a bone vibrator (bone conduction) and varies its level using the classic **Hughson-Westlake** up-5-down-10 procedure to find the softest level the patient detects at least half the time. Each ear is tested separately and marked with standard symbols: a **red O for the right ear** and a **blue X for the left ear** (a convention from maritime navigation lights). Severity bands are: **normal 0-25 dB HL**, **mild 26-40**, **moderate 41-55**, **moderately severe 56-70**, **severe 71-90**, and **profound above 90 dB HL**. A flat trace near the top means normal hearing; a trace that slopes downward toward the right is the classic high-frequency loss seen in aging and noise exposure.

slides.title: Why these scientists matter to the clinic
slides.body:
Each historical figure left a fingerprint on everyday clinical practice, so it is worth connecting names to consequences.

**Harvey Fletcher** and **Wilden Munson** gave us the understanding that loudness is not the same as physical intensity. Their **1933 equal-loudness contours** showed that the ear is far more sensitive around **2-4 kHz** than at the extremes of the audible range. This is why the **dB HL** scale on the audiogram is *frequency-corrected*: the raw sound-pressure level needed to reach threshold differs by tens of decibels across frequency, but dB HL subtracts that out so that normal hearing reads as a flat line near zero. Without the Fletcher-Munson insight there would be no principled zero reference for the audiogram.

**Georg von Bekesy** explained *where* in the cochlea different pitches are encoded. His **traveling wave** demonstrated **tonotopy**: high frequencies peak near the **base** of the cochlea (the stiff end, close to the **oval window**) and low frequencies near the **apex** (the floppy end). This place principle is why noise damage and aging tend to harm high-frequency hearing first — the basal region is mechanically and metabolically the most vulnerable. Von Bekesy also lent his name to **Bekesy audiometry**, an automatic self-tracking threshold method.

**Raymond Carhart** built the clinic itself. Beyond founding the academic discipline at **Northwestern University**, he described the **Carhart notch** — a characteristic dip in bone-conduction thresholds around **2000 Hz** seen in **otosclerosis**, a stiffening of the **stapes** footplate. Recognizing this notch on an audiogram still helps clinicians distinguish a fixable middle-ear problem from inner-ear damage.

Later institutions extended the work. The **American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA)** and the **American Academy of Audiology (AAA)**, founded in **1988**, professionalized the field; the doctoral **Au.D.** degree became the standard clinical credential. Internationally, the **World Health Organization (WHO)** estimates that over **1.5 billion** people live with some hearing loss, framing audiology as a global public-health priority. From **Fletcher** and **Munson** measuring telephone listeners, to **von Bekesy** peering into the cochlea, to **Carhart** rehabilitating veterans, the audiogram became the shared language that ties all of this together: a simple chart that encodes a century of physics, physiology, and care.

question.question: On a standard audiogram, why is **0 dB HL placed at the top** of the vertical axis with louder thresholds plotted downward?
options: Because sound intensity is measured on a negative scale.

Because **dB HL** is referenced to the average threshold of normal-hearing young adults, so 0 dB HL represents the best (normal) hearing, and larger numbers represent poorer thresholds that need louder sounds to detect; plotting them downward makes a worse hearing trace sink lower on the chart.
Because high frequencies are always louder than low frequencies.
Because the bone-conduction vibrator outputs negative pressure.
question.explanation: **dB HL (Hearing Level)** is calibrated against the average normal young-adult threshold (per ANSI S3.6 / ISO 389). Normal hearing is therefore about 0 dB HL at every frequency, placed at the top. A person who needs a louder tone to reach threshold has a higher dB HL number representing poorer hearing, and the convention plots these downward so that a worse audiogram visibly sinks toward the bottom.

hints: Think about what reference defines 0 dB HL.
Better hearing means you can detect quieter tones, i.e. a smaller dB HL number.
slides.workedSolution: dB HL is defined relative to the average threshold of normal-hearing young adults, so by construction normal hearing sits at roughly 0 dB HL across frequency and occupies the top of the chart. Poorer hearing requires louder tones, giving larger dB HL values that are plotted downward, so a sinking trace immediately signals worse hearing.

question.question: A patient's audiogram droops on the right side of the chart.
question.prompt: A 68-year-old retired carpenter has an audiogram that is near 5-10 dB HL at 250, 500, and 1000 Hz but falls to 50 dB HL at 4000 Hz and 60 dB HL at 8000 Hz in both ears. Using the place principle that von Bekesy established, explain why high-frequency thresholds are the ones that have worsened, and predict which kinds of speech sounds this person will struggle to hear.

question.question: Pure-tone audiometry uses octave-spaced test frequencies. Starting from **250 Hz**, an octave is a doubling of frequency. What test frequency, in Hz, is **two octaves above 250 Hz**?
question.hint: One octave doubles the frequency: 250 to 500 is one octave; double again for the second octave.

question.question: Match the scientist to the contribution most directly underlying clinical audiology.
options: Georg von Bekesy published the 1933 equal-loudness contours at Bell Labs.
Raymond Carhart received the 1961 Nobel Prize for the cochlear traveling wave.

Harvey Fletcher and Wilden Munson described the equal-loudness contours (1933) at Bell Labs; Georg von Bekesy demonstrated the cochlear traveling wave and won the 1961 Nobel Prize; Raymond Carhart founded clinical audiology after World War II at Northwestern.
Wilden Munson invented the cochlear implant during World War II.
question.explanation: Fletcher and Munson produced the equal-loudness contours (1933) that justify the frequency-corrected dB HL scale. Von Bekesy explained the cochlear traveling wave (Nobel 1961), grounding tonotopy. Carhart, working with WWII veterans at Northwestern, founded clinical audiology and described the Carhart notch. The other options scramble these attributions.

hints: Only one person here won a Nobel Prize, and it was for inner-ear mechanics.
The equal-loudness contours came in pairs of names from Bell Labs.
slides.workedSolution: Fletcher and Munson: equal-loudness contours, 1933, Bell Labs. Von Bekesy: cochlear traveling wave, Nobel Prize 1961. Carhart: father of clinical audiology, post-WWII, Northwestern University, and the Carhart notch of otosclerosis. The correct option is the one stating all three accurately.

question.question: Interpreting symbols on an audiogram.
question.prompt: You are handed an audiogram showing a series of red O symbols hovering around 10 dB HL across all frequencies, and a series of blue X symbols that drop from 15 dB HL at 250 Hz to 70 dB HL at 8000 Hz. Explain what the colors and symbols mean, which ear has the problem, and how you would describe the severity of that ear's loss at 8000 Hz using the standard severity bands.
